stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted an app without the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file, which became mandatory for all apps submitted after February 2025. The app used Required Reason APIs (UserDefaults, file timestamp access, disk space) without declaring the reasons in a privacy manifest.
stories.whatAppleSaid: ITMS-91053: Missing API declaration - Your app's code in the binary references one or more APIs that require reasons. Starting February 2025, all apps must include a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file that declares the reasons for using Required Reason APIs. Please add the privacy manifest to your app.
stories.fix: Created a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file and added it to the app target's Build Phases > Copy Bundle Resources. Declared all Required Reason API usages with their approved reasons (e.g., NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults with reason 'CA92.1' for app functionality). Also ensured all third-party SDKs included their own privacy manifests.
behavioralSignals: Required Reason API usage without manifest

stories.guidelineName: Data Use and Sharing - Required Reason APIs
stories.rejectionReason: Your PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file exists in the project but is not included in the app bundle.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Created the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file and added it to the Xcode project, but forgot to add it to the target's Build Phases > Copy Bundle Resources. The file existed in the project navigator but was not included in the compiled app bundle.
stories.whatAppleSaid: ITMS-91053: Missing API declaration - Your app references Required Reason APIs but the privacy manifest was not found in the app bundle. Please ensure the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file is included in your app's Copy Bundle Resources build phase.
stories.fix: Added the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file to the correct target's Build Phases > Copy Bundle Resources. Verified it was included in the bundle by inspecting the .ipa contents. For frameworks and Swift packages, ensured each target has its own privacy manifest included in the correct location.
behavioralSignals: PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy in project but not bundle
file not in Copy Bundle Resources

stories.guidelineName: Data Collection and Storage - Account Deletion
stories.rejectionReason: Your app supports account creation but does not offer account deletion.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built an app with user registration and login but did not provide any way for users to delete their account and associated data from within the app. Users had to email support to request account deletion.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.1(v) - Legal - Privacy - Data Collection and Storage: Apps that support account creation must also offer account deletion. Your app allows users to create an account but does not provide the ability to delete the account within the app. The account deletion option must be easy to find and must initiate deletion of the account and all associated personal data.
stories.fix: Added an 'Delete Account' option in Settings > Account. The deletion flow includes a confirmation dialog explaining what data will be deleted, a re-authentication step for security, and an optional reason selector. Account and all associated data are deleted within 14 days as per Apple's requirements. Also added the AccountDeletionURL in App Store Connect.

stories.rejectionReason: The App Tracking Transparency prompt does not appear on iPad during review.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Implemented ATT (App Tracking Transparency) permission request, but it only appeared on iPhone. On iPad, the ATT prompt never showed because the app was checking for IDFA availability using an older API that returned different results on iPad, or the prompt was being called before the app was in the active state on iPad.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: We noticed that your app does not display the App Tracking Transparency permission prompt on iPad. The app appears to collect tracking data without requesting user permission. Please ensure the ATT prompt appears on all supported device types.
stories.fix: Ensured the ATT prompt is called after the app reaches the active state using applicationDidBecomeActive or sceneDidBecomeActive. Added a delay to ensure the UI is fully loaded before presenting the prompt. Tested on both iPhone and iPad to verify the prompt appears correctly on all devices.

stories.rejectionReason: The App Tracking Transparency prompt is called at an inappropriate time and does not display.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Called requestTrackingAuthorization() in application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:) or during a scene transition, before the app was fully in the foreground active state. The system silently dropped the ATT prompt because the app wasn't yet active.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: The App Tracking Transparency prompt does not appear when your app is launched. The ATT prompt must be displayed while the app is in the active state. Please ensure you request tracking authorization at an appropriate time after the app has become active.
stories.fix: Moved the ATT permission request to trigger after the app is fully active and visible. Used a slight delay (e.g., DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 1.0)) after applicationDidBecomeActive to ensure the app is ready. Showed the prompt on a meaningful screen (e.g., after onboarding) rather than immediately on launch.

stories.rejectionReason: The App Tracking Transparency prompt is blocked by other permission dialogs.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Requested multiple permissions simultaneously on app launch: notifications, location, camera, and ATT. The system queued these permission dialogs, and on some devices/OS versions the ATT prompt was blocked or dismissed by other permission alerts appearing over it.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: We were unable to see the App Tracking Transparency prompt during our review. It appears that other permission requests may be interfering with the ATT prompt display. Please ensure the ATT prompt is displayed without interference from other system dialogs.
stories.fix: Implemented a sequential permission request flow that spaces out permission prompts. Request permissions one at a time with appropriate delays between each. Show the ATT prompt on its own screen without other system dialogs. Used a permission queue manager to ensure only one system alert is presented at a time.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app uses a third-party SDK (Adjust) that performs device fingerprinting for tracking purposes.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Used the Adjust SDK for attribution tracking. An older version of the SDK performed device fingerprinting (collecting device model, OS version, IP address, locale, and other signals to create a unique identifier) as a fallback when IDFA was unavailable, violating Apple's anti-tracking policies.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: Your app includes a third-party SDK (Adjust) that collects device and usage data to create a unique identifier for tracking purposes (fingerprinting). Fingerprinting is not permitted regardless of whether the user has granted tracking permission. Over 50,000 apps were affected by this enforcement action.
stories.fix: Updated the Adjust SDK to the latest version that complies with Apple's anti-fingerprinting requirements. The updated SDK removes fingerprinting fallback mechanisms and relies solely on ATT-consented IDFA or Apple's SKAdNetwork for attribution. Verified with Adjust's compliance documentation.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app's photo library permission description does not adequately explain why the app needs access.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Set the NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription to a vague message like 'App requires photo access to function' or 'This app needs your photos' without explaining specifically why the app needs photo library access and how the photos would be used.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.1 - Legal - Privacy - Data Collection and Storage: Your app's permission request descriptions are not sufficiently descriptive. The purpose string for photo library access ('App requires photo access to function') does not clearly explain to users why the app needs this access. Please provide a specific, clear description of how the app uses the photo library.
stories.fix: Updated NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription to a specific, clear description: 'YourApp needs access to your photo library to let you select photos for your profile picture and share images in chat conversations.' The description now explains exactly what the photos are used for.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app accesses the photo library without including the required NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: The app's own code didn't access the photo library, but a third-party SDK (e.g., an image picker library, chat SDK, or analytics SDK with screenshot detection) included photo library access APIs. The developer didn't add NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription to Info.plist because they were unaware the SDK accessed photos.
stories.whatAppleSaid: ITMS-90683: Missing Purpose String in Info.plist - Your app's code references the photo library API but the corresponding purpose string (NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription) is not present in the Info.plist. All apps that access the photo library must include a purpose string explaining the use.
stories.fix: Added NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription to Info.plist with a clear description of how the third-party SDK uses photo access. Audited all third-party SDKs for permission requirements and ensured all required usage descriptions are present. Alternatively, if the photo access was unnecessary, configured the SDK to disable that feature or switched to an SDK that doesn't require photo access.

stories.rejectionReason: Your VPN app uses the VPN capability primarily for content blocking or ad blocking rather than providing a VPN service.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Created an app that used the Network Extension VPN entitlement primarily to block ads, trackers, and specific website content by routing traffic through a local VPN tunnel with DNS-level filtering. The app was marketed as an ad blocker rather than a VPN service.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.4 - Legal - VPN Apps: Your app uses the VPN capability for purposes other than providing a virtual private network service. Using the VPN entitlement primarily for content blocking, ad blocking, or traffic manipulation is not permitted. VPN apps must provide VPN service as their primary function.
stories.fix: Restructured the app to use Safari Content Blocker extension (Content Blocker API) for ad blocking instead of VPN-based filtering. For DNS-level filtering, used the DNSSettings configuration profile approach. Removed the VPN entitlement since the app's primary purpose was content blocking, not VPN.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app's privacy policy URL leads to a broken page or placeholder content.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Provided a privacy policy URL in App Store Connect that returned a 404 error, was a placeholder page ('Coming Soon'), or redirected to the app's homepage without any privacy policy content.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.1 - Legal - Privacy - Data Collection and Storage: The privacy policy URL provided for your app does not lead to a valid privacy policy. The URL returns a 404 error. All apps must provide a working privacy policy URL that is accessible to users.
stories.fix: Created a proper privacy policy page and hosted it at a stable, permanent URL. Ensured the URL is accessible, loads quickly, and contains a complete privacy policy. Updated the privacy policy URL in App Store Connect and within the app settings.
behavioralSignals: broken link in App Store Connect

stories.rejectionReason: Your privacy policy does not adequately describe the data your app collects and how it is used.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Provided a generic one-paragraph privacy policy that did not specify what data the app collects, how it's used, whether it's shared with third parties, data retention periods, or user rights regarding their data.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.1 - Legal - Privacy - Data Collection and Storage: Your privacy policy does not adequately describe your app's data collection and usage practices. The privacy policy must clearly identify what data is collected, how it is used, when it is shared, and the data retention policy. Please update your privacy policy to include these details.
stories.fix: Rewrote the privacy policy to include: specific types of data collected (personal info, usage data, device info), purposes of data collection, third-party services and SDKs that receive data, data retention and deletion policies, user rights (access, correction, deletion), contact information for privacy inquiries, and effective date.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app accesses location data in the background for analytics purposes rather than a user-facing feature.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Requested 'Always' location permission and tracked the user's location in the background to feed location data into an analytics platform for market research, without providing any user-facing feature that required background location.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: Your app collects location data in the background for analytics and advertising purposes rather than providing a user-facing feature. Background location access must be tied to a feature that directly benefits the user. Using location for analytics or advertising is not a valid use of background location.
stories.fix: Removed background location tracking entirely. Downgraded to 'While Using' location permission. Location data is now only used for the app's core map feature while the user is actively using the app. Removed location data from the analytics pipeline.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app reads clipboard contents without clear user intent or action.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: The app read the clipboard contents (UIPasteboard.general.string) on every app launch or foreground event to detect URLs, referral codes, or other content. Starting with iOS 16, users see a paste notification banner and starting with iOS 14, a paste indicator appears, making this behavior highly visible.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.1 - Legal - Privacy - Data Collection and Storage: Your app reads the clipboard contents on launch without a clear user action or intent. Reading clipboard data should only occur in response to an explicit user action (e.g., tapping a paste button). Automatically reading the clipboard on app launch is not permitted.
stories.fix: Removed automatic clipboard reading on launch. Implemented a 'Paste' button that users can tap to voluntarily share clipboard contents. Used the new UIPasteboard.DetectionPattern API (iOS 14+) to detect if the clipboard contains relevant content (like URLs) without actually reading it, then show a prompt for the user to paste.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app shares user data with third-party SDKs that are not disclosed in your privacy nutrition labels.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Integrated multiple third-party SDKs (analytics, advertising, crash reporting) that collected and shared user data, but did not disclose this data sharing in the App Privacy (nutrition label) section of App Store Connect. The privacy labels showed 'Data Not Collected' while SDKs were actively collecting and transmitting user data.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 5.1.2 - Legal - Privacy - Data Use and Sharing: Your app's privacy information on the App Store does not accurately reflect your app's data collection and sharing practices. We identified third-party SDKs in your app that collect data not disclosed in your privacy nutrition labels. Please update your App Privacy information to accurately reflect all data collection.
stories.fix: Audited all third-party SDKs for data collection practices using each SDK's privacy documentation. Updated the App Privacy nutrition labels in App Store Connect to accurately reflect all data collected by the app and its SDKs, including the purpose of collection and whether it's linked to the user's identity.
behavioralSignals: privacy labels don't match SDK data collection
Data Not Collected but SDKs present

stories.rejectionReason: We discovered one or more bugs in your app. Your app crashed during our review.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted an app that had a race condition in the initialization sequence. The app worked fine locally but crashed on first launch when network conditions were slower, which matched Apple's review environment.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We discovered one or more bugs in your app when reviewed on iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 17.2. Specifically, the app crashed on launch. Please review the crash logs attached in the resolution center.
stories.fix: Analyzed the crash log from the resolution center. Found a force-unwrap on an optional that was nil when a network request hadn't completed before the UI tried to access the data. Added proper nil-checking and async/await handling for the initialization sequence. Tested on a clean install with network throttling enabled.
behavioralSignals: works locally but crashes in review

stories.rejectionReason: Your app includes placeholder content. Apps should be complete and fully functional when submitted for review.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted an app where some secondary screens still contained 'Lorem ipsum' placeholder text, sample images, and TODO comments visible in the UI. The developer forgot to replace placeholder content before submission.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app includes placeholder content that makes it appear as though the app is not yet complete. Specifically, we found Lorem ipsum text on the About page and placeholder images in the settings screen. Please complete all content before resubmitting.
stories.fix: Replaced all Lorem ipsum text with real content. Replaced placeholder images with production assets. Did a full audit of every screen to ensure no remaining placeholder content, TODO labels, or sample data was visible.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app references TestFlight or beta testing in the production build.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Left a 'Thank you for beta testing!' banner and a 'Report Beta Bug' button visible in the production build. The app also had a settings toggle labeled 'TestFlight Debug Mode' that was visible to all users.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app contains references to TestFlight and beta testing, which is not appropriate for the production version of your app. Specifically, we found a 'Report Beta Bug' button and references to TestFlight in the settings. Please remove all beta-related content.
stories.fix: Wrapped all beta/TestFlight-related UI elements in compile-time flags (#if DEBUG) and runtime checks for TestFlight environment. Removed the beta testing banner and debug toggle from the production build configuration.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app does not work on IPv6-only networks as required.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Hardcoded IPv4 addresses for API server connections instead of using domain names. Apple's review network uses a NAT64/DNS64 environment (IPv6-only), causing all direct IPv4 connections to fail.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We discovered one or more bugs in your app when reviewed on iPad running iOS 17.1 on an IPv6 network. Specifically, the app was unable to load content. Apps must support IPv6-only networking as many carrier networks are IPv6-only.
stories.fix: Replaced all hardcoded IPv4 addresses with domain name-based connections. Used NSURLSession/URLSession which handles IPv6 natively. Tested using Apple's NAT64 test network setup (macOS Internet Sharing with 'Create NAT64 Network' enabled) to verify connectivity.
behavioralSignals: works on WiFi but fails in review

stories.rejectionReason: Your app failed to connect to its server when tested on Apple's IPv6 review network.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: The app used a third-party networking library that had a bug with NAT64 address synthesis. It worked on the developer's local IPv6 test setup but failed on Apple's specific NAT64/DNS64 configuration because the library was manually resolving DNS instead of letting the system handle it.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app was unable to connect to its server during review. The app displayed a 'Connection Error' message when attempting to load the main feed. We tested on an IPv6 network and were unable to use the app's core functionality.
stories.fix: Updated the third-party networking library to the latest version which fixed the NAT64 compatibility issue. Switched from manual DNS resolution to system-provided APIs (getaddrinfo) that properly handle IPv6 address synthesis. Verified using Apple's recommended NAT64 testing setup.
behavioralSignals: works locally but fails in review

stories.rejectionReason: Your app declares audio background mode but does not play audio content.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Added the UIBackgroundModes 'audio' capability to keep the app alive in the background for periodic data syncing, even though the app had no audio playback functionality.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.5.4 - Performance - Software Requirements: Your app declares the audio background mode in UIBackgroundModes but does not include audio playback functionality. The audio background mode is intended only for apps that provide audible content to the user. Using background modes for purposes other than their intended function is not permitted.
stories.fix: Removed the 'audio' UIBackgroundMode. Implemented proper background data syncing using BGTaskScheduler (BGAppRefreshTask and BGProcessingTask) which is the correct API for periodic background work without requiring audio playback.

stories.rejectionReason: We were unable to sign in to your app with the demo account provided because it required two-factor authentication.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Provided demo account credentials in the App Review notes, but the account had mandatory two-factor authentication enabled which sent an SMS code to the developer's phone. The Apple reviewer had no way to receive the 2FA code.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We were unable to complete the review of your app because we could not sign in using the demo credentials provided. The account requires two-factor authentication via SMS, and we were unable to receive the verification code. Please provide demo credentials that allow full access without requiring additional verification steps.
stories.fix: Created a dedicated demo/review account with 2FA disabled. Added the demo credentials (username, password) in the App Review Information section of App Store Connect. Included a note explaining which features to test and any special instructions for the reviewer.
behavioralSignals: unable to sign in during review

stories.rejectionReason: We were unable to sign in using the magic link authentication because the link expired before we could use it.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Implemented passwordless authentication using magic links sent via email. When the Apple reviewer opened the email on iPad, the Mail app's link preview/prefetch feature automatically triggered the magic link URL, consuming it before the reviewer could manually tap it to authenticate.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We were unable to complete the login process. We received the magic link email, but when we tapped the link it showed 'Link expired or already used.' We attempted this multiple times with the same result.
stories.fix: Changed the magic link flow to a two-step process: the link now opens a confirmation page in the browser where the user must tap 'Confirm Sign In' before the token is consumed. This prevents email client prefetching from invalidating the link. Also added a fallback OTP code option as an alternative to magic links.

stories.rejectionReason: Passkey creation failed during our review. The app displayed an error when attempting to create a passkey.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Implemented passkey (WebAuthn) authentication but the Apple App Site Association (AASA) file wasn't being fetched quickly enough by Apple's CDN during the review. The passkey creation requires the AASA file to be available at /.well-known/apple-app-site-association to verify the domain-app association.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We were unable to create a passkey during review. When attempting to register, the app displayed 'Unable to create passkey. Please try again later.' We attempted multiple times without success.
stories.fix: Ensured the AASA file was properly hosted and cached before submission. Added the associated domains entitlement with the webcredentials service. Pre-warmed the AASA cache by making requests to the domain before submission. Also added a fallback email/password registration option so reviewers could complete onboarding even if passkey creation failed.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app includes the ability to download and execute code after installation, which can be used to introduce features not reviewed by Apple.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Used Microsoft CodePush (or a similar hot-code-push solution) to push JavaScript bundle updates to a React Native app, bypassing the App Store review process. The updates were capable of changing app functionality beyond minor bug fixes.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3.1 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your app contains hidden features. Specifically, your app includes functionality that allows for the remote downloading and execution of code that can change the app's behavior or functionality after review. Apps must not provide mechanisms to alter their primary functionality post-review.
stories.fix: Configured CodePush to only push minor bug fixes and UI text changes, not functional changes. Added documentation in the review notes explaining that CodePush is used only for critical bug fixes and does not alter app functionality. Some developers choose to remove CodePush entirely and use standard App Store updates instead.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app is missing the required app icon.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted an app without including the 1024x1024 App Store icon in the asset catalog, or the icon was corrupted/transparent. The app appeared with a blank or default icon in App Store Connect.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your app is missing the required 1024x1024 App Store icon. All apps must include a valid app icon that will be displayed on the App Store. Please add the icon to your app's asset catalog.
stories.fix: Added the 1024x1024 App Store icon to the Assets.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset. Verified all required icon sizes were present and none were transparent or contained alpha channels (which App Store Connect rejects).

stories.rejectionReason: Your macOS app's release notes reference iOS-specific features and terminology.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Jesse Squires' Taxatio app was a universal app supporting both iOS and macOS. The release notes for a macOS update mentioned iOS-specific features like 'improved iPhone widget' and 'haptic feedback improvements' that don't apply to macOS.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your Mac app's release notes reference iOS-specific features ('iPhone widget', 'haptic feedback'). Release notes for macOS apps should be relevant to the macOS version of your app.
stories.fix: Created platform-specific release notes. For macOS submissions, wrote release notes that only reference macOS-relevant features and improvements. Used App Store Connect's platform-specific metadata fields to provide different release notes for each platform.
behavioralSignals: iOS terms in macOS release notes
platform-specific features mentioned for wrong platform

stories.rejectionReason: Your app's screenshots do not accurately reflect the current version of your app.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted an app update with significant UI changes but forgot to update the App Store screenshots. The screenshots showed the old design with a tab bar at the bottom, while the new version used a sidebar navigation pattern.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3.7 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your app's screenshots do not reflect the current version of your app. The screenshots show a different navigation pattern and UI layout than what is present in the current build. Please update your screenshots to accurately represent the app.
stories.fix: Took new screenshots on all required device sizes reflecting the current UI. Used Xcode's screenshot automation or a tool like fastlane snapshot to generate consistent screenshots across all required device sizes and localizations.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app preview poster frame contains the word 'Free' which references pricing.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Created an app preview video whose poster frame (the still image shown before the video plays) contained text overlay saying 'Try Free for 7 Days'. Apple prohibits pricing references in app preview content.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your app preview includes references to your app's price. Specifically, the poster frame contains the text 'Try Free for 7 Days.' App previews and screenshots may not reference pricing information, as pricing can vary by region and may change over time.
stories.fix: Removed the 'Try Free for 7 Days' text from the app preview poster frame and video. Replaced it with a value-proposition message like 'Track Your Fitness Goals' that describes app functionality without referencing pricing.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app's version number suggests it is a pre-release or beta version.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted the first version of an app with version number '0.1' or '0.9.2-beta', suggesting the app was not yet a complete, finished product ready for the App Store.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app version number (0.1) suggests that the app is still in development or beta stage. Apps submitted to the App Store should be final versions. Please update your version number to reflect a production-ready release (e.g., 1.0).
stories.fix: Changed the version number from '0.1' to '1.0.0' in the project settings and App Store Connect. Removed any 'beta' or 'pre-release' suffixes from the version string and marketing version.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app appears to have debug or development mode features visible to users.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Submitted a production build with debug logging visible in a console view, a floating debug menu accessible via a hidden gesture, and network request/response details displayed in an overlay that could be triggered by shaking the device.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app includes development tools and debug information that are visible to users. Specifically, shaking the device reveals a network debugging overlay and there is a hidden debug menu accessible through a multi-tap gesture. Please remove all development/debugging features from the production build.
stories.fix: Wrapped all debug UI elements in #if DEBUG preprocessor directives. Removed the shake-to-debug gesture recognizer from the release build. Ensured the debug menu is only accessible in development builds by checking the build configuration at runtime.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app attempts to connect to localhost or development server URLs.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Accidentally shipped a production build with the API base URL still pointing to 'http://localhost:3000' or a staging server like 'https://staging-api.example.com'. The app failed to load any content during review because the development server was not accessible.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app was unable to load content during our review. We found that the app is attempting to connect to development/staging server URLs that are not accessible. Please ensure your app connects to production servers.
stories.fix: Fixed the build configuration to use the correct production API URL. Implemented environment-based configuration using .xcconfig files or build schemes so that Debug/Staging/Release builds automatically use the correct server URLs. Added a runtime check that warns during development if production URLs are not configured.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app downloads large amounts of data after installation without informing the user.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Published a game that was 150MB on download but immediately required an additional 2GB asset download on first launch without any disclosure in the App Store listing or a user prompt before downloading.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.3 - Performance - Accurate Metadata: Your app downloads a significant amount of additional content (approximately 2GB) after installation without informing the user beforehand. Users should be informed about the total storage requirements. Please disclose the additional download requirement in your app description and provide a prompt before downloading.
stories.fix: Added a note in the App Store description about the additional download size. Implemented a pre-download prompt showing the total size and allowing the user to choose when to download. Added a progress indicator showing download status and the option to download over Wi-Fi only.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app has an incomplete user interface. A purchase/subscription page appears blank.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: The app's premium subscription page was blank during review because the StoreKit products hadn't been approved in App Store Connect yet, or the product IDs were misconfigured. The reviewer saw an empty paywall with no pricing or subscription options displayed.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: Your app appears to be incomplete. Specifically, the subscription page does not display any content - it appears as a blank screen with no purchase options. Please ensure all pages in your app are fully functional.
stories.fix: Ensured all IAP products were in 'Ready to Submit' or 'Approved' status in App Store Connect before submitting the app for review. Added error handling and a fallback UI for when StoreKit products fail to load, showing a 'Unable to load products. Please try again.' message with a retry button instead of a blank screen.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app crashed during review due to a system framework issue, but the rejection still stands.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: The app crashed during review due to a known bug in Apple's own UIKit framework (specifically a UICollectionView layout crash on certain iOS versions). The developer filed a Radar/Feedback but the crash still caused a rejection because Apple reviews based on observed behavior, not cause.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 2.1 - Performance - App Completeness: We discovered one or more bugs in your app. The app crashed when navigating to the gallery view. While we understand this may be related to a system framework issue, apps must not crash regardless of the underlying cause.
stories.fix: Implemented a workaround for the UIKit framework bug by using a different collection view layout approach. Added a try-catch wrapper around the problematic layout code and a fallback layout in case of failure. Filed a Feedback Assistant report with Apple about the underlying framework bug.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app includes user-generated content but does not include the required moderation controls.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built an education app (FlipLearn) with a social feed where students could post content, but did not include any report, block, or flag buttons on posts or user profiles.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.2 - Safety - User-Generated Content: Your app enables the display of user-generated content but does not have the required precautions in place. Specifically, your app is missing the ability to report objectionable content, block abusive users, and a mechanism to flag content for review.
stories.fix: Added a flag/report button on every post and user profile, implemented user blocking functionality, added a 24-hour content moderation SLA with a dedicated moderation queue, and included a visible link to community guidelines.

stories.rejectionReason: Your Kids Category app includes third-party analytics with the ability to collect identifiable information from minors.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Published a kids educational game in the Kids Category on the App Store while including Firebase Analytics SDK, which can collect device identifiers and behavioral data in violation of COPPA regulations.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.3 - Safety - Kids Category: Your app includes third-party analytics software with the ability to collect and transmit identifiable information about children. Specifically, we found your app integrates Firebase Analytics which may collect device identifiers. Apps in the Kids Category must not include third-party analytics or advertising that can collect identifiable information.
stories.fix: Removed Firebase Analytics SDK entirely from the app. Replaced with a custom first-party analytics solution that collects only anonymous aggregate event counts stored on the developer's own server, with no device identifiers or user-level tracking.

stories.rejectionReason: Your Kids Category app includes third-party analytics (Amplitude) which may collect identifiable information from children.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Integrated Amplitude analytics SDK in a children's learning app listed in the Kids Category to track user engagement and session metrics.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.3 - Safety - Kids Category: We found that your app uses the Amplitude SDK, which has the capability to collect identifiable information. Apps in the Kids Category may not include third-party analytics or third-party advertising. You must remove all such SDKs before resubmitting.
stories.fix: Removed Amplitude SDK completely. Built a lightweight custom event tracker that only logs anonymized session durations and feature usage counts without any device fingerprinting, IDFA, or persistent identifiers.
behavioralSignals: third-party analytics present in Kids Category app

stories.rejectionReason: Your app connects users anonymously for video chat, which presents a high risk of pornographic or objectionable content.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built a Chatroulette-style anonymous video chat app that randomly paired strangers for live video conversations with no content filtering or identity verification.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.1.4 - Safety - Objectionable Content: Your app facilitates anonymous video connections between users, which creates significant risk for pornographic content, exploitation, and abuse. Apps that connect strangers for anonymous communication must implement robust safeguards including content moderation and age verification.
stories.fix: The developer was unable to adequately address Apple's concerns. Anonymous random video chat apps are effectively banned from the App Store due to the inherent risk of objectionable content. The developer pivoted to a moderated, interest-based matching system with AI-powered nudity detection, mandatory profile verification, and real-time content monitoring.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app provides drug dosage calculations but is not from a recognized institution such as a drug manufacturer, hospital, or university.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: An independent developer built a drug dosage calculator app for healthcare professionals that calculated dosages based on patient weight, age, and renal function without affiliation to any medical institution.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.4.2 - Safety - Medical: Your app provides drug dosage calculations. Per App Store Review Guidelines, drug dosage calculators must come from the drug manufacturer, a hospital, university, health insurance company, pharmacy, or other approved entity. We are unable to accept drug dosage calculators from independent developers due to the potential risk to patient safety.
stories.fix: The developer partnered with a university hospital's pharmacy department, which agreed to co-publish the app under the hospital's developer account with clinical pharmacist review and validation of all dosage formulas.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app contains content that requires a higher age rating than what is currently set in App Store Connect.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Published a card game app with simulated gambling mechanics (poker chips, betting) and cartoon combat violence, but set the age rating to 4+ in App Store Connect without properly answering the content description questionnaire.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.1 - Safety - Objectionable Content: Your app contains simulated gambling and frequent/intense cartoon violence, but the age rating is set to 4+. You must update your age rating in App Store Connect to accurately reflect the content in your app. Please review the content descriptions and adjust accordingly.
stories.fix: Updated the App Store Connect age rating questionnaire to accurately reflect simulated gambling (selecting 'Frequent/Intense') and cartoon violence (selecting 'Frequent/Intense'), which raised the age rating to 12+.

stories.rejectionReason: App collected children's email addresses for in-game rewards without verifiable parental consent.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: TinyCo's kids games prompted children to enter their email addresses to receive virtual game items and rewards, collecting personal information from minors without obtaining verifiable parental consent as required by COPPA.
stories.whatAppleSaid: This case resulted in an FTC settlement rather than a standard App Review rejection. The FTC found TinyCo violated COPPA by collecting children's email addresses without parental consent. Apple subsequently tightened enforcement of Guideline 1.3 for all Kids Category apps.
stories.fix: TinyCo paid a $300,000 FTC settlement and removed all email collection prompts from kids games. Implemented age-gating and parental consent flows for any data collection. This case became a precedent for stricter Kids Category enforcement.
behavioralSignals: email input field in kids game

stories.rejectionReason: Your app contains objectionable content including vulgar and profane language.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Ninjawords, a dictionary app, was rejected because it contained definitions for vulgar and profane words. The developer had to strip out thousands of dictionary entries that Apple deemed objectionable, even though the app was a reference dictionary.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Your application contains content that many audiences would find objectionable. Specifically, the dictionary includes definitions for terms that are vulgar, profane, and sexually explicit in nature. You must remove this content or implement a content filter.
stories.fix: The developer removed objectionable word definitions from the dictionary database and submitted a censored version. This case sparked public controversy about Apple's content policies, as critics argued a dictionary should be allowed to define all words. Apple later softened its stance on reference content when properly age-rated.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app enables users to rate the physical appearance of real people, which is considered mean-spirited and objectionable.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built a Hot-or-Not style app where users could upload photos of real people and other users would vote on their attractiveness with a rating system.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.1.1 - Safety - Objectionable Content: Your app allows users to rate the physical appearance of other people, which Apple considers to be mean-spirited and potentially harmful. This type of content that objectifies real individuals is not appropriate for the App Store.
stories.fix: The concept was fundamentally incompatible with Apple's guidelines. The developer pivoted to a photo contest app where users voluntarily submitted their own photos to themed photography challenges judged on artistic merit rather than personal appearance.

stories.rejectionReason: Your app references being designed for kids in its metadata but is not published in the Kids Category.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Published an app outside the Kids Category but included phrases like 'perfect for kids' and 'designed for children ages 3-8' in the app description and marketing text. The app also did not comply with Kids Category data collection restrictions.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.3 - Safety - Kids Category: Your app's metadata indicates it is designed for children, but it is not published in the Kids Category. Apps that are designed specifically for children must be published in the Kids Category and must comply with all Kids Category requirements, including restrictions on data collection, third-party analytics, and advertising.
stories.fix: The developer had two choices: either move the app to the Kids Category and comply with all Kids Category requirements (removing third-party analytics, advertising, and external links), or remove all references to children from the app description and metadata. They chose to move to the Kids Category and strip out non-compliant SDKs.

stories.rejectionReason: Your Kids Category app includes third-party advertising which is not permitted.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Published a children's coloring book app in the Kids Category that displayed AdMob banner ads and interstitial ads between activities. The ads were not age-appropriate and included tracking.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.3 - Safety - Kids Category: Your app includes third-party advertising (Google AdMob) in a Kids Category app. Apps in the Kids Category may not include third-party advertising or analytics. All ads in Kids Category apps must be appropriate for children and must not include behavioral targeting or tracking.
stories.fix: Removed Google AdMob SDK entirely. Switched to a premium paid model with no ads. For developers who need ad revenue in Kids Category apps, Apple requires using Apple's own advertising framework (SKAdNetwork) with certified kid-safe ad content from Apple-approved networks.
behavioralSignals: behavioral ad targeting in children's app

stories.rejectionReason: Your app with user-generated content does not include terms of service that users must agree to.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built a community forum app where users could post text and images but did not include any terms of service, community guidelines, or content policy that users were required to accept before participating.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.2 - Safety - User-Generated Content: Your app enables users to share content but does not include published terms of service or community guidelines. Apps with user-generated content must include terms that clearly state what content is not acceptable and the consequences of violations.
stories.fix: Added a Terms of Service and Community Guidelines document within the app. Implemented a mandatory acceptance flow during onboarding where users must agree to the terms before being able to post content. Added a link to the terms in the app settings.
behavioralSignals: users can post without accepting rules

stories.rejectionReason: Your medical app does not include appropriate disclaimers about the limitations of its health-related information.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Created a symptom checker app that provided potential diagnoses based on user-entered symptoms without any medical disclaimers, warnings that the information is not a substitute for professional medical advice, or recommendation to consult a healthcare provider.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.4.1 - Safety - Physical Harm: Your app provides medical information and symptom analysis without appropriate disclaimers. Medical apps must clearly indicate that the information provided is not intended to replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. You must include prominent disclaimers throughout the app.
stories.fix: Added a prominent disclaimer on the app's launch screen and before every symptom analysis result stating 'This app is for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare provider.' Also added a persistent disclaimer banner on all diagnosis result screens.
behavioralSignals: diagnosis results without professional consultation reminder

stories.rejectionReason: Your app promotes tobacco and/or alcohol products without implementing an age verification gate.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Built a craft beer discovery app that showcased various alcohol brands, included purchasing links, and featured tobacco-related lifestyle content without any age verification or age gate on app launch.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.1.5 - Safety - Objectionable Content: Your app facilitates the sale or promotion of tobacco and alcohol products but does not include an age gate. Apps that promote or sell age-restricted products must include an appropriate age verification mechanism to ensure users meet the minimum legal age requirements.
stories.fix: Implemented an age gate on first launch requiring users to confirm they are of legal drinking age (21+ in US). Added date-of-birth verification with persistent storage so users only need to verify once. Also added age-appropriate content warnings on alcohol-related pages.
behavioralSignals: alcohol content displayed without age check

stories.rejectionReason: Your social media app does not include a mechanism for users to report objectionable content.
stories.whatDeveloperDid: Launched a photo-sharing social media app with commenting and messaging features but only included content moderation on the backend. There was no user-facing way to report posts, comments, or other users for objectionable content.
stories.whatAppleSaid: Guideline 1.2 - Safety - User-Generated Content: Your app includes user-generated content features such as photo sharing and commenting but does not provide a mechanism for users to report objectionable content and abusive users. You must implement a reporting mechanism that is easily accessible to users.
stories.fix: Added a three-dot menu on every post and comment with a 'Report' option. Added a 'Report User' button on user profiles. Implemented a report flow with categories (spam, harassment, inappropriate content, etc.) and confirmation. Also added an in-app content moderation dashboard for the team.

1.1.name: Objectionable Content
1.1.summary: Apps must not include content that is offensive, insensitive, upsetting, or in exceptionally poor taste, including defamatory content or realistic portrayals of violence. Apple reviews this content on a case-by-case basis.

1.1.1.name: Objectionable Content - Defamatory or Mean-Spirited
1.1.1.summary: Apps may not include defamatory, discriminatory, or mean-spirited content about religion, race, sexual orientation, gender, or national or ethnic origin, particularly content likely to humiliate, intimidate, or harm a targeted individual or group.

1.1.4.name: Objectionable Content - Pornography
1.1.4.summary: Apps may not include overtly sexual or pornographic material, defined as explicit descriptions or displays of sexual organs or activities intended to stimulate erotic rather than aesthetic or emotional feelings.

1.1.5.name: Objectionable Content - Religious Commentary
1.1.5.summary: Apps may not include inflammatory religious commentary or inaccurate or misleading quotations of religious texts.

1.2.name: User-Generated Content
1.2.summary: Apps with user-generated content must include a method to filter objectionable material before it posts, a mechanism to report content and abusive users with a timely response, the ability to block abusive users, and published contact information so users can reach the developer.

1.3.name: Kids Category
1.3.summary: Apps in the Kids Category must not include links out of the app, purchasing opportunities, or other distractions unless placed behind a parental gate, and must not send personally identifiable information or device information to third parties, including third-party analytics or advertising.

1.4.1.name: Physical Harm
1.4.1.summary: Medical and health apps that could provide inaccurate data or be used for diagnosing or treating patients are reviewed with greater scrutiny, and must clearly disclose the data and methodology supporting any health measurement or diagnostic claims.

1.4.2.name: Physical Harm - Drug Dosage Calculators
1.4.2.summary: Drug dosage calculators must come from the drug manufacturer, a hospital, university, health insurance company, pharmacy, or other approved entity, or must receive approval from the FDA or an equivalent national body.

2.1.name: App Completeness
2.1.summary: Submissions must be final versions with all necessary metadata and fully functional URLs included, and must not contain placeholder text, empty websites, or other temporary content. Apps that crash or exhibit obvious bugs are rejected under this guideline.

2.3.name: Accurate Metadata
2.3.summary: App metadata, including the description, screenshots, and previews, must accurately reflect the app's core experience so customers know what they are getting before they download or buy it.

2.3.1.name: Accurate Metadata - Hidden or Undocumented Features
2.3.1.summary: Apps may not include hidden, dormant, or undocumented features. All functionality must be described with specificity in the Notes for Review, and the app must not be marketed in a way that promotes content or services it does not actually provide.

2.3.7.name: Accurate Metadata - App Name and Keywords
2.3.7.summary: App names are limited to 30 characters and keywords must accurately describe the app. Developers may not pack metadata with trademarked terms, competitor app names, prices, or other irrelevant phrases just to game search results.

2.5.1.name: Software Requirements
2.5.1.summary: Apps may only use public APIs and must run on the currently shipping OS. Developers must keep apps up to date and phase out deprecated features, frameworks, or technologies rather than relying on unsupported or insecure configurations.

2.5.4.name: Software Requirements - Background Modes
2.5.4.summary: Multitasking apps may only use background services for their intended purposes, such as VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, or local notifications. Declaring background modes the app does not genuinely need is not permitted.

3.1.1.name: In-App Purchase
3.1.1.summary: Apps that unlock features or functionality within the app must use in-app purchase to collect payment. Apps may not use their own mechanisms, such as license keys, QR codes, or cryptocurrency, to unlock content or functionality.

3.1.2.name: Subscriptions
3.1.2.summary: Auto-renewable subscriptions must provide ongoing value to the customer, must last at least seven days, and must be available across all of the user's devices. Apps must also implement a restore mechanism for previously purchased subscriptions.

3.1.3.name: Other Purchase Methods
3.1.3.summary: Certain app types, such as reader apps, multiplatform services, enterprise services, person-to-person services, and apps selling physical goods or services consumed outside the app, may use purchase methods other than in-app purchase.

3.1.5.name: Cryptocurrencies
3.1.5.summary: Apps may facilitate virtual currency storage only when offered by a developer enrolled as an organization, and apps may not mine for cryptocurrency on the device unless the processing happens off device, such as cloud-based mining.

3.1.5(b).name: Cryptocurrencies
3.1.5(b).summary: Crypto wallets may only be offered by developers enrolled as organizations. Apps may not mine cryptocurrency on the device, exchange features may only be offered by the exchanges themselves, and ICO or token sale functionality must come from established financial institutions in compliance with local law.

3.2.name: Other Business Model Issues
3.2.summary: Apps must follow acceptable business practices. Apps may not artificially increase impressions or click-throughs of ads, and apps designed predominantly for the display of ads are not permitted.

3.2.2.name: Other Business Model Issues - Unacceptable
3.2.2.summary: Unacceptable business practices include creating an interface for browsing third-party apps or extensions similar to the App Store, artificially inflating ad impressions or click-throughs, and collecting charitable or fundraising donations unless the developer is an approved nonprofit.

4.0.name: Design
4.0.summary: Apple expects apps to be simple, refined, and easy to use, meeting minimum design standards for approval. Apps that stop working or offer a degraded experience after approval may be removed from the App Store at any time.

4.1.name: Copycats
4.1.summary: Developers should submit original ideas. Apps that simply copy another popular app, or make minor changes to another app's name, UI, or functionality and pass it off as original, are not permitted.

4.2.name: Minimum Functionality
4.2.summary: Apps should include features, content, and UI that elevate them beyond a repackaged website. An app that is not particularly useful, unique, or app-like does not belong on the App Store.

4.3.name: Spam
4.3.summary: Developers may not create multiple bundle IDs of the same app or submit apps that are indistinguishable from what is already widely available. Certain categories, such as flashlight or simple timer apps, will not be accepted unless they offer a meaningfully different experience.

4.5.3.name: Apple Sites and Services
4.5.3.summary: Apps must not use Apple services, including Game Center, Push Notifications, and Live Activities, to spam, phish, or send unsolicited messages to customers.

4.8.name: Login Services
4.8.summary: Apps that use a third-party or social login service to set up or authenticate the user's primary account must also offer an equivalent login option that limits data collection to the user's name and email, allows email to stay private, and does not collect interactions for advertising without consent.

5.1.1.name: Data Collection and Storage
5.1.1.summary: All apps must include a link to their privacy policy that clearly and explicitly identifies what data the app collects, how it is collected, all uses of that data, and the app's data retention and deletion policies.

5.1.1(v).name: Account Deletion
5.1.1(v).summary: Apps that let people use them without a login should do so unless the app has significant account-based features. Apps that support account creation must also offer account deletion from within the app, not only by contacting support.

5.1.2.name: Data Use and Sharing
5.1.2.summary: Apps may not use, transmit, or share a person's data without first obtaining permission, and data collected for one purpose may not be repurposed without further consent unless otherwise permitted by law.

5.1.3.name: Health and Health Research
5.1.3.summary: Apps may not use or disclose data gathered in health, fitness, or medical research contexts to third parties for advertising, marketing, or other use-based data mining purposes unrelated to improving health management or the research itself.

5.1.4.name: Kids
5.1.4.summary: Apps primarily designed for kids must comply with children's privacy statutes such as COPPA and GDPR-K, must handle any personal data from minors with heightened care and parental consent where required, and may not send personally identifiable information or device information from kids apps to third parties.

5.3.4.name: Gaming, Gambling, and Lotteries
5.3.4.summary: Apps that offer real money gaming such as sports betting, poker, casino games, or lotteries must have the necessary licensing and permissions in every location where the app is used, must be geo-restricted to those locations, and must be free on the App Store.

5.4.name: VPN Apps
5.4.summary: Apps offering VPN services must use the NetworkExtension framework, may only be offered by developers enrolled as an organization, and must provide VPN service as their primary function rather than using the VPN entitlement mainly for content or ad blocking.
